subChunks.title: React DevTools and Debugging Techniques
subChunks.hookHtml: Bugs are inevitable. The difference between a developer who flails and one who finds the root cause in five minutes is tooling and technique. React DevTools gives you a window into the component tree, current props, and live state. Combined with deliberate console strategies and a systematic mental model, most bugs collapse quickly.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
React DevTools — the component inspector

Install the React DevTools browser extension (Chrome / Firefox). It adds two panels to your browser DevTools:

  • Components — browse the component tree, see current props and state for any component, even edit them live
  • Profiler — record renders and see which components re-rendered, why, and how long they took

The Components panel is your most-used debugging tool. Click any component to see:

  • All its current props
  • All its current state values (useState hooks listed in order)
  • The hooks it uses
  • What component rendered it (the parent)

Vex: "Before adding a single console.log, open the Components panel and click the component that isn't working. 80% of the time the bug is visible right there: the prop has the wrong value, or state is null when it shouldn't be."

Effective console.log strategies

When you need to log, be deliberate:

// ❌ Ambiguous — what is this?
console.log(user);

// ✅ Labelled — clear in the console
console.log('UserCard user:', user);

// ✅ Multiple values at once:
console.log({ user, isLoading, error });

// ✅ Tracing renders:
console.log('UserCard rendered'); // appears every render

// ✅ Conditional logging during development
if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development') {
  console.log('Quest list state:', quests);
}

Why does my component render too many times?

Each of these causes a re-render:

  • State changed (via a setter)
  • A prop changed
  • The parent re-rendered (by default, children re-render with the parent)
  • A context value changed

Add a console.log('ComponentName render') at the top of the component body (not inside a handler). Count how many times it fires. In development with StrictMode, React intentionally double-renders — this is normal and expected.

Isolating the problem — the binary search method

When a complex component doesn't work:

  1. Comment out half the JSX. Does the bug still happen? If not, the bug is in the commented half.
  2. Restore half the commented code. Does the bug reappear? Binary search until you've isolated the exact line.
  3. Once isolated, check the props and state of that element in DevTools.

Common bugs and how to spot them

Component doesn't re-render after state update:
Open DevTools — is state actually changing? If yes but no re-render, you're mutating instead of replacing.

Wrong data displayed:
Check the prop value in DevTools. Is the prop correct? If yes, the display logic is wrong. If no, the parent is passing the wrong value.

Undefined errors on first render:
State or prop is undefined during the first render before data loads. Add a guard: if (!user) return null; or use optional chaining: user?.name.

Event handler not firing:
Check the element in the browser DevTools (not React DevTools) — is the event listener attached? Is there an overlapping element blocking clicks?

// Defensive rendering for async data:
function UserProfile({ userId }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);

  // ...loading logic...

  if (!user) return <p>Loading...</p>; // guard against null

  return <h1>{user.name}</h1>; // safe to access now
}

storyBeats.text: Vex pulls a jeweller's loupe from her coat pocket and holds it over a tangled circuit diagram. 'You cannot fix what you cannot see,' she says. 'DevTools is the loupe.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: When something doesn't work, do not guess. Open the Components panel. Find the component. Look at its props and state. The answer is almost always visible before you write a single line of debugging code. Guessing is slow. Looking is fast.

storyBeats.speaker: Labelled console logging

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Below is a buggy component — it renders a counter but clicking 'Increment' does nothing, and a null-access error appears when the initial data is missing. Fix both bugs:

  • Bug 1: The increment handler mutates state instead of replacing it — fix the setter call
  • Bug 2: The component crashes when user prop is null — add a guard clause
  • Add a data-testid="count" on the count display and a data-testid="name" on the user name display

guidedPracticeTests.label: Renders without crash when user is null
Renders user name when user provided

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <DataInspector> component from scratch. It takes an arbitrary data prop (any object or array). Render a <pre> element showing the data as formatted JSON (JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)). Handle the case where data is null or undefined — display "No data" text instead. Add a toggle button that shows/hides the inspector panel.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Describe your debugging process when a React component renders blank or shows wrong data. Walk through the steps in order — starting with DevTools, then console strategies, then code-level fixes. Explain why checking props/state in DevTools before adding console.log is faster.

questions.prompt: What does the React DevTools Components panel show?
options: The component tree with current props and state for any selected component
The compiled JavaScript output React sends to the browser
Network requests made by React components
CSS styles applied to each React component's root element
questions.answer: The component tree with current props and state for any selected component
questions.explanation: The Components panel renders a tree of all mounted React components. Clicking any component shows its current props, state (from useState hooks), context values, and the hooks it uses. You can even edit props and state live. This is the primary tool for diagnosing rendering bugs without needing to add console.log statements.

questions.prompt: A component renders blank but no error is thrown. What is the most efficient first debugging step?
options: Open React DevTools Components panel, select the component, and inspect its current props and state
Add console.log statements throughout the component to trace execution
Delete the component and rewrite it from scratch
Check the browser's Network tab for failed API requests
questions.answer: Open React DevTools Components panel, select the component, and inspect its current props and state
questions.explanation: The Components panel shows you the actual props and state at render time. A blank render usually means a prop is null or undefined, or state is an empty array when it shouldn't be. Seeing this takes 5 seconds in DevTools. Adding console.log takes longer and produces the same information. Rewriting is never the first step. Network issues cause data problems but the symptom is visible in props/state first.

questions.prompt: In development, a component renders twice for every state change. What is the most likely cause?
options: React StrictMode intentionally double-renders components in development to surface side effects
There is an infinite loop in the component's logic
The component is registered as a child in two places in the component tree
console.log is calling a state setter which triggers additional renders
questions.answer: React StrictMode intentionally double-renders components in development to surface side effects
questions.explanation: StrictMode (enabled by default in Create React App and Vite templates) wraps the app and deliberately renders components twice in development only. This helps expose side effects that depend on render order or count. It's intentional and expected — the extra renders do not happen in production. An infinite loop would cause hundreds of renders (and usually a stack overflow), not exactly two.
